paragraphs.text: This is a love poem where nobody describes love — instead, love gets performed. A separated woman speaks. She appeals to a passing cloud. And the landscape answers her mood: peacocks cry when clouds come, and that is not decoration, it is part of what makes the feeling real. Literary theory calls these the determinants of the mood.

Here is the device that made this poem the first of its genre: the cloud is never actually told to carry any message. That meaning hangs unsaid — and the unsaid part is the whole point. The voice does not end in despair either. It ends in sustaining memory: her love is kept alive by remembering his goodness. So love, the abiding feeling, transforms sorrow — which is only passing through — into something you can actually savor. Meanwhile the events: desire wakes in the heart to kill, and the absent beloved rises right along with it. The cAtaka bird, who drinks only rain, begs water. The peacocks sound at the clouds. And she is protected by nothing but remembrance of his virtue.
